Photo Credit: Duma.gov.ru, Wikipedia Commons Opinion 1 Europe Social Issues September 20, 2026 September 20, 2026 Paul Goble 0 Comments By Paul Goble Key Takeaways: Not just a stamp. Aleksey Uvarov (RIDL) says Putin’s Duma is no longer a public fight among regions and ministries, but after February 2022 loyalty is the test and real bargains—budgets, regulation, security turf, jobs—happen before the floor vote. Abstentions matter more than “no.” Still does work. He lists leftover jobs: drafting, administration, representation, personnel, and quiet lobbying for governors and sectors. Calling it useless, he argues, mistakes vote totals for the whole machine. A shell that can refill. Ceremonial bodies can matter again if the outside shock hits—he cites the RSFSR Supreme Soviet after the 1990 competitive elections. In a succession crisis, ready rules and offices could take on politics again; do not write them off as dead. Under Putin, the Duma has been transformed from a place where regional and bureaucratic interests were fought out in public to a tightly controlled branch of the power vertical; and as a result, many are inclined to write it off as an irrelevancy, according to Aleksey Uvarov. The Russian political scientist argues that the Duma has continued to “perform functions invisible if one looks only at vote totals and points out that abstentions rather than voting no have become more frequent but no less important in terms of what happens under today’s tighter Kremlin control ( ridl.io/ru/parlament-mobilizovannogo-gosudarstva/ ). Since February 2022 when Putin launched his expanded war against Ukraine, Uvarov continues, “political loyalty has become a standalone criterion for the state apparatus” and for the Duma, which no longer is where policies are debated but where the very real conflicts of interests in the system are addressed more quietly but all the same in very real ways. He reminds that “an authoritarian system does not eliminate conflicts of interests: it changes how they are resolved. Ministries still compete for resources, governors for federal funding, big business for regulatory terms, security agencies for powers, and political groups for personnel slots.” But now, those differences must be settled before a floor vote. What that means is that it is incorrect to call the Duma today “a purely useless institution,” Uvarov says. On the one hand, it “still performs administrative, legislative, representative and personnel functions and can be a venue for advancing regional or sectional interests” and promoting the advancement of its members. And on the other, institutions like the Duma which have been reduced to “performing mainly ceremonial bodies or ratifying the decisions of others can quickly acquire independent political significance when the external environment shifts. The experience of the RSFSR Supreme Soviet is instructive.” “For most of the Soviet period, the RSFSR Supreme Soviet almost automatically endorsed party leadership decisions, but after competitive elections to the Congress of People’s Deputies in 1990, the situation changed within months,” Uvarov says. The same thing could happen with the Duma during a succession crisis. And he concludes: “Formally existing institutions should not be written off as definitively dead merely because, under the current political configuration, they are subordinated to the executive. If that configuration changes, ready‑made procedures, offices, and representative structures can again be filled with political content.” About Paul Goble Paul Goble is a longtime specialist on ethnic and religious questions in Eurasia. Most recently, he was director of research and publications at the Azerbaijan Diplomatic Academy. Earlier, he served as vice dean for the social sciences and humanities at Audentes University in Tallinn and a senior research associate at the EuroCollege of the University of Tartu in Estonia. He has served in various capacities in the U.S. State Department, the Central Intelligence Agency and the International Broadcasting Bureau as well as at the Voice of America and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty and at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. https://hvg.hu/vilag/20261116_zelenszkij.text: Az utolsó csepp a pohárban az Uszty-Luga-i kikötő elleni támadás volt, ahol leégett öt üzemanyagtartály és három helikopter, valamint egy hajó is megsemmisülhetett. A Kreml-közeli hadibloggerek Telegram-csatornáin már napok óta terjed a hír, hogy Oroszország Nemzetbiztonsági Tanácsa (Szovbez) a legfelsőbb ukrán vezetés kiiktatását követeli – írja a Meduza . Szombaton a Moszkovszkij Komszomolecben jelent meg cikk arról, hogy döntés született Zelenszkij megöletéséről, mint írják, a biztonsági szolgálatok vezetői meggyőzték Vlagyimir Putyint arról, hogy végezni kell az ukrán felső vezetéssel, köztük Zelenszkijvel is. A cikkben szerepel az is, hogy a döntéshez vezető utolsó csepp a pohárban a Leningrádi körzetben található Uszty-Luga kikötője elleni szerdai ukrán dróntámadás volt, amelynek a végső mérlege egyelőre nem ismert. Annyit tudni, hogy öt üzemanyagtartály égett le, továbbá az ukrán drónok sikerrel támadták a rakétafegyverzettel ellátott Naro-Fominszk korvettet is. A nem hivatalos orosz beszámolók szerint a hajó megsemmisült, és három helikopter is a pilótáikkal együtt. A Moszkovszkij Komszomolec szerint a döntést a Szovbez ülésén azzal magyarázták, hogy az ukrán drónok elleni passzív védelmi stratégia nem működik, és ezért a dróntámadások elrendelőit kell célba venni. Az oroszok azt állítják, hogy eddig nem akartak végezni Zelenszkijvel, ugyanakkor az elmúlt évekből legalább három eset már nyilvánosságra került, amikor mégis megpróbálták. Először nem sokkal a háború kitörését követően, amikor 2022 márciusának elején közölték az ukránok, hogy egy csecsen kommandó és az FSZB két csoportja is megpróbált végezni az ukrán elnökkel. Az ukrán elhárítást, az SZBU-t vezető Vaszil Maljuk pedig tavaly nyáron arról beszélt , hogy szervezete két Zelenszkij elleni merényletet is meghiúsított. Az egyiket Lengyelországban követte volna el egy oroszok által beszervezett nyugalmazott lengyel katona, akit a lengyel szolgálatokkal együttműködve lepleztek le az ukránok. A másik esetről annak idején mi is beszámoltunk , ekkor az oroszok az ukrán kormányőrség vezetőjét, egy ezredest szerveztek be, és Vlagyimir Putyin elnöki beiktatására időzítették volna a merényletet. A terv az volt, hogy akkor csapnak le Zelenszkijre, amikor az elnök belép az irodájába. A kormányőrség parancsnoka mellett egy másik ezredest is letartóztattak az ügyben. Akár 15 év börtönt is kaphat a korrupciós pénzt több ügyféltől is a gyanú szerint elfogadó hivatali dolgozó.

Photograph: Leonardo Muñoz/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Shares in Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, were on Friday worth hardly more than when they listed. Photograph: Leonardo Muñoz/AFP/Getty Images Stock markets Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? Lauren Almeida and Graeme Wearden Fri 20 Nov 2026 16.38 EST First published on Fri 20 Nov 2026 05.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut. Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began. 11:06 Is Claude creator Anthropic really worth $1.3 trillion? - The Latest US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap. Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? Read more Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.” Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%. The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies. In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI. European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low. The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO . View image in fullscreen South Korea’s Kospi index lost 5.5% at end of trading. Photograph: Yonhap/EPA Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion “The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said. Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout. Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending. “The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.” Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China. Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war. Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March. Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.
